notes.meaning: The prophet sees a mighty warrior approaching from Edom and its capital city, Bozrah, dressed in glorious, blood-stained robes and marching with great power. When asked who He is, the warrior answers that He is the Lord, faithful to His word and mighty to deliver His people. This reveals that the Lord Himself comes to crush evil and bring victory to those who trust Him. Believers can rest in the knowledge that God is both righteous and able to save.

differ.view: John Calvin taught that this passage describes God Himself judging the enemies of the church without human help, rather than Christ stained with His own blood on the cross.
Charles Spurgeon understood the majestic warrior to be Jesus Christ returning in triumph over spiritual and earthly enemies.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critical scholars view verses 1–6 as a separate poem that was placed here independently of the surrounding text.

notes.meaning: The onlooker asks why the warrior's garments are stained bright red like the clothes of someone who has been stomping grapes in a wine trough. Pressing grapes would splash red juice all over a worker's clothes, but here the red color comes from the blood of battle. God is willing to take on what looks like lowly and difficult work to defeat the oppressors of His people.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church writers such as Cyprian saw the red garments as a figure of Christ's suffering, whose blood had to be poured out like pressed wine so that believers could receive it.

notes.meaning: The conqueror answers that He trampled the winepress completely alone because none of the nations stood with Him. In His righteous anger He crushed His adversaries until their lifeblood splattered all over His garments. This means that God alone carries out the final judgment against evil without needing any human aid. God alone is the ultimate rescuer and judge of the world.

differ.view: John Calvin insisted that this verse describes God executing vengeance on Edom without earthly assistance, and argued that applying it to Christ making atonement alone distorts the text.

notes.meaning: The warrior explains that the time for punishing wicked oppressors was fixed in His heart, and the set time to rescue His chosen people had finally arrived. The judgment on the enemy is called a single day, while the season of rescue and favor for His people is pictured as a whole year. God never forgets His promise to deliver His suffering children from harm.

The Lord looked around and was stunned that no human being rose up to help or defend the oppressed. Because there was no one to give support, His own almighty arm accomplished the rescue, fueled by His righteous anger against evil. When all human helpers fail, God's own strength is more than enough to save.

The Lord stomped out rebellious nations in His anger and made them stagger helplessly as if they were drunk from a cup of wrath. He poured out their lifeblood onto the ground to break their power completely. No earthly force can stand when God rises to hold cruel rulers accountable for their sins.

The prophet begins a prayer by recounting the Lord's faithful covenant love and the many wonderful deeds He has performed. God poured out rich blessings on the people of Israel because of His deep pity and boundless mercy. Recalling what God has done in the past brings comfort and strength when present times are hard.

The Lord chose Israel to be His very own people, expecting them to act like honest children who would remain loyal to His covenant. Because of this family bond of love, He stepped in to be their Savior in their times of trouble. God desires sincere loyalty from those who bear His name.

Whenever the people were in pain, the Lord shared their affliction, and the Angel of His Presence came to rescue them. In His tender love and pity He bought them back from slavery, carrying them safely through all the days of old. God cares deeply about our personal troubles and walks beside us in our darkest trials.

differ.view: John Calvin held that the Angel of His Presence refers to a created ministering angel rather than to Christ Himself.

notes.meaning: The people turned away from God and brought deep grief to His Holy Spirit through their stubborn murmuring and rebellion. Because of their unfaithfulness, the Lord turned against them and fought as their opponent to bring them to repentance. Sin hurts God's heart and invites His loving discipline upon our lives.

In their suffering, the people remembered the ancient days of Moses and asked where their great Rescuer had gone. They wondered where the God was who had brought their ancestors safely through the Red Sea with their leaders and placed His Holy Spirit among them. Looking back at past miracles stirs up faith and a desire to return to the Lord.

The people recalled how God's glorious power stood at Moses' right hand and split the waters of the sea right before their eyes. The Lord did this extraordinary wonder to make His name known forever as the true Deliverer. Everything God does to save His people is meant to bring eternal praise to His holy name.

The Lord led the whole nation through the deep seabed as smoothly and safely as a horse running across an open desert plain. Even though the path was completely new, God smoothed the way so that no one tripped or fell. God clears a level path for His people through situations that seem impossible.

Just as tired cattle are guided down into a peaceful, green valley to rest, the Spirit of the Lord brought His weary people into the rest of the promised land. God gently led Israel through the desert to make Himself a glorious name among the nations. The Lord brings His people through long, tiring journeys into places of spiritual rest and safety.

The prayer begs the Lord to look down from His holy and majestic home in heaven upon His needy people. The speaker asks where God's burning zeal and mighty strength have gone, wondering why His tender compassion seems held back. God invites His people to speak honestly to Him when His help feels far away.

The community appeals to the Lord as their real Father, admitting that earthly forefathers like Abraham and Jacob are dead and cannot help them. They know that God is their true Father whose ancient name is their Redeemer. When human helpers can do nothing, believers can always rely on God's unchanging fatherly care.

differ.view: John Calvin explained that this verse does not mean the dead saints have no care for us, but rather stresses that God remains our Father even if all earthly parents disown us.
John Gill noted that because the patriarchs are dead and cannot know our earthly needs, believers are taught to stop relying on lineage and put all their trust in God alone.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: George Leo Haydock explained that Abraham would not acknowledge ungodly descendants as his true children, nor does he possess the divine power to rescue them.

notes.meaning: The prayer cries out asking why the Lord has permitted His people to stray from His ways and let their hearts become too hardened to fear Him. The speaker pleads with God to return in mercy for the sake of His servants and the people He chose as His special inheritance. When we sense our own spiritual hardness, we should ask God to soften our hearts and draw near again.

differ.view: John Calvin taught that God judicially hardens the impenitent by handing them over to Satan, acting as an active judge rather than simply allowing sin.
Franz Delitzsch explained that when people stubbornly reject divine grace, God judicially withdraws it and leaves their hearts incapable of faith.
John Gill held that the godly here mourn that God had withheld the restraints of His grace, leaving them to wander, without making God the author of sin.

notes.meaning: The people grieve that they enjoyed the holy land for only a short time compared to God's eternal covenant promises. Cruel foreign enemies had marched in and trampled down the Lord's holy temple. Losing sacred places of worship brings deep sorrow to those who love God's presence.

The broken nation laments that they now seem like pagan peoples whom God never ruled and who never carried His holy name. Their miserable state makes it appear as though the covenant bond had been completely forgotten. Even in times of deepest abandonment, God's people can remind Him that they belong to Him.
